Step-by-Step Audio Guided Tour: French Riviera biking tour
Tour-Category: biking

Stop 1: Cap Ferrat

Address: Saint-Jean-Cap-Ferrat, 06230 Villefranche-sur-Mer

Coordinates: 43.6804, 7.3193

Type/Specialty: Scenic coastal spot

Specific Examples: Cliffside views, historic villas, Mediterranean gardens

Orientation: You are about to embark on a cycling journey through the French Riviera. Pedaling from Cap Ferrat to the Massif de l'Esterel, spanning approximately 47 kilometers of coastal landscapes and storied streets, we'll trace a path through opulence and natural beauty. Discover forgotten tales of espionage, artistic inspiration, and coastal transformation as we weave through this captivating region. From Picasso's art studio in Antibes to the Cannes Film Festival's iconic venue at La Croisette, uncover how history intertwines with daily life in the enchanting region. As you journey through the upcoming stops, you'll learn about Maugham's attempt to adopt his secretary at Saint-Jean-Cap-Ferrat Peninsula Loop and Brigitte Bardot's iconic bikini appearance at La Croisette. Your first stop is Cap Ferrat. Head southeast on the main road towards the coast, passing through charming coastal villages. Position yourself to best view this location.

Cap Ferrat, known for its tranquility and luxurious allure, has been a magnet for the rich and famous. In the early 1900s, King Leopold II of Belgium acquired half of Cap Ferrat, using the wealth he amassed from the Congo. This acquisition marked the beginning of the area's development into an exclusive retreat. In 1900, he met Blanche Delacroix, a 16-year-old French courtesan, adding layers of intrigue to the luxurious setting. Fast forward to 1927, Somerset Maugham, the renowned British writer, purchased Villa La Mauresque. This villa became a backdrop for Maugham’s personal life and literary endeavors. He lived there openly with his younger companions, first Gerald Haxton and later Alan Searle. By the 1960s, Maugham ensured his legacy was as dramatic as his stories. In a public spectacle, he legally adopted Alan Searle, effectively disinheriting his daughter, Liza, and making Searle his sole heir. This legal maneuvering highlighted the complexities of Maugham's personal life, leaving a notable imprint on the villa’s history. Another intriguing chapter of Cap Ferrat's past involves the artist Jean Cocteau. Invited for a weekend stay at Villa Santo Sospir by Francine Weisweiller in 1950, Cocteau ended up residing there for twelve years. During his extended stay, he transformed the villa into a living canvas, adorning its walls with murals that carried his distinctive artistic vision. This creative endeavor left an indelible mark on the villa, intertwining Cocteau's legacy with the place. As you continue your journey around Cap Ferrat, the whispers of its storied past accompany you, revealing how this captivating peninsula has been a canvas for personal stories and artistic expression.

Directions: Start your ride from Cap Ferrat and pedal eastward along the beautiful coastal road. As you bike along, you'll pass by the iconic Villa Ephrussi de Rothschild. Continue riding until you reach the loop around the Saint-Jean-Cap-Ferrat Peninsula, where you can enjoy stunning views of the Mediterranean Sea.Stop 2: Saint-Jean-Cap-Ferrat Peninsula Loop

Address: Villefranche-sur-Mer, 06230, France

Coordinates: 43.6962, 7.3076

Type/Specialty: Biking trail with panoramic views

Specific Examples: Azure waters, lush vegetation, hidden coves

Orientation: As you cycle along the Saint-Jean-Cap-Ferrat Peninsula Loop, pause just before the path dips towards the lighthouse.

The year was 1899 when King Leopold II of Belgium's scandalous liaison with the young Blanche Zélia Joséphine Delacroix stirred the whispers of Europe. Their affair, which began here, became a public spectacle, culminating in their secret marriage on his deathbed in 1909. This union ignited a fierce legal battle with his daughters over his estates, a drama that unfolded under the gaze of the Riviera's sunlit shores. The echoes of this past linger in the salty air, a reminder of how personal desires can ripple into public affairs, leaving their mark on more than just paper and ink. A different kind of story unfolded here in the late 1920s when the renowned author W. Somerset Maugham made Villa La Mauresque his home. Seeking to secure his legacy, Maugham controversially attempted to adopt his secretary, Alan Searle, in a bid to prevent his own daughter from inheriting his estate. This decision, fraught with legal disputes, erupted into a major inheritance war in the 1960s. The olive trees here seem to murmur the secrets of these bygone days, their leaves rustling with the weight of familial conflict and the quest for control. As you continue along this historic loop, the peninsula reveals its many hidden pathways, each turn offering glimpses into lives once lived amid the splendor o. Just ahead, the cobblestones of history pave the way to Antibes, where the stories of past and present converge in the ongoing dance of time and tide.

Directions: Pedal eastward from Saint-Jean-Cap-Ferrat Peninsula Loop, enjoying the coastal breeze as you ride past Villa Ephrussi de Rothschild. Follow the scenic route towards Nice, then continue biking along the Promenade des Anglais. As you approach Antibes Old Town, cycle through the charming streets until you reach the historic ramparts and Port Vauban.

Stop 3: Antibes Old Town

Address: 06600 Antibes, France

Coordinates: 43.5804, 7.1251

Type/Specialty: Historic town center

Specific Examples: Medieval architecture, Picasso Museum, vibrant market

Orientation: Position yourself to best view this location.

Antibes Old Town is a tapestry of stories, woven through its narrow streets and picturesque squares. In 1946, the illustrious Pablo Picasso found himself drawn to this locale, transforming the 14th-century Château Grimaldi into his personal art studio. Faced with a post-war shortage of traditional art supplies, Picasso turned to marine boat enamel and industrial plywood, materials that remarkably aligned with his innovative spirit. These creations, born out of necessity, marked a unique chapter in his artistic journey, capturing the essence of Antibes through an unconventional lens. Picasso was not the only figure to leave a mark on Antibes. In 1982, the writer Graham Greene cast a shadow over the glamorous Riviera with his pamphlet 'J’Accuse: The Dark Side of Nice.' This publication was a direct response to the troubling experiences faced by Martine Cloetta, the daughter of Greene's mistress, who found herself entangled with local organized crime. Greene's writings brought attention to the darker undercurrents beneath the sun-drenched facade of the Riviera, challenging the perception of this picturesque region. In 1915, the town became a hotspot for bootlegging after the French government banned absinthe. Local fishermen, ever resourceful, used hidden Roman cellars to move contraband, weaving a tale of defiance against authority. This spirit of rebellion was echoed by a 19th-century mayor, who was allegedly caught storing illicit spirits beneath the marketplace and reportedly pacified town guards with anise-flavored bribes. Antibes Old Town is not just a place of ancient stones but a canvas for stories of creativity and intrigue. As you cycle away from the historic core, the modern allure o beckons, yet the echoes of Antibes' past linger, reminding you of a town where art and audacity have long danced together under the Mediterranean sun.

Directions: Hop on your bike and pedal down Avenue de Verdun towards the coast. Ride along the scenic coastal road, Boulevard de la Croisette, all the way to La Croisette in Cannes. Enjoy the beautiful views of the Mediterranean Sea as you cycle towards your destination.

Stop 4: La Croisette

Address: Boulevard de la Croisette, 06400 Cannes

Coordinates: 43.5499, 7.0174

Type/Specialty: Famous promenade

Specific Examples: Luxury boutiques, sandy beaches, Palais des Festivals

Orientation: Position yourself to best view this location.

La Croisette is where 's allure crystallizes, blending history with modern opulence. Once a simple street along the Mediterranean, it has evolved into a glamorous stage for the Cannes Film Festival, where stories of fame and intrigue unfold. In 1953, Brigitte Bardot made headlines when she appeared on the Croisette sands in a bikini, a bold fashion statement that launched her into international stardom and cemented the Riviera's reputation for beach glamor. This singular moment not only elevated Bardot's career but also positioned the Côte d'Azur as a beacon of elegance and allure. Further enriching its tapestry of tales, the Carlton Hotel stands as an architectural emblem of La Croisette's storied past. Designed by Charles Dalmas in 1911, the hotel boasts twin cupolas, said to be inspired by La Belle Otero, a renowned Spanish courtesan. This unique design choice speaks to the era's fascination with opulence and the colorful characters who frequented the Riviera. Fast forward to July 2013, when the Carlton became the scene of a jaw-dropping diamond heist. An Israeli diamond magnate was showcasing his rare jewels when a lone thief made off with $136 million worth of diamonds in under two minutes, a theft that captured global attention and added another chapter to the hotel's notorious history. As you continue along the boulevard, the juxtaposition of the shimmering Mediterranean against the backdrop of chic establishments echoes the Riviera's dual heritage of natural beauty and cultural significance. Moving past the city's lights, the road will eventually lead toward the natural splendor of the Esterel, promising yet another facet of this region's diverse narrative.

Directions: Hey there! Starting from La Croisette, pedal west along the beautiful coastal road Avenue du Maréchal Juin. Enjoy the stunning views as you ride towards the Massif de l'Esterel. Once you reach the mountain range, you can explore the scenic biking trails weaving through the red rocks and lush greenery. Happy cycling!

Stop 5: Massif de l'Esterel

Address: Massif de l'Esterel, 83700 Saint-Raphaël

Coordinates: 43.4599, 6.8651

Type/Specialty: Red volcanic mountain range

Specific Examples: Hiking trails, panoramic views, rugged terrain

Orientation: Position yourself to best view this location.

Amidst this natural spectacle, the Corniche d’Or weaves its tale. Conceived in 1901 by Abel Ballif, the first president of the Touring Club de France, this scenic route was more than a road; it was a vision to connect and celebrate the beauty of the Côte d'Azur. Completed in 1903, the Corniche d’Or linked Saint-Raphaël to Cannes, a route you have recently visited. In the shadow of Mont Vinaigre, the highest peak of the massif standing at 618 meters, history whispers its own tales. The notorious Gaspard Bouis, known as Gaspard de Besse, found refuge here in the late 18th century. A Robin Hood figure of his time, Bouis hid among these hills until his capture in 1780 led to his execution in Aix-en-Provence. His story lingers, a reminder of the lawless days when these crags sheltered outlaws and rebels. Fast forward to the mid-20th century, and these shores bore witness to another kind of storm. On August 15, 1944, the Plage du Débarquement at Le Dramont became the staging ground for Operation Dragoon. Over 20,000 soldiers from the U.S. 36th 'Texas' Infantry Division stormed ashore, carving a path for the liberation of Southern France from German occupation. This pivotal moment in World War II history left an indelible mark on the landscape and its people. The road beckons you onward, each turn promising more tales and vistas to capture.

That's 5 stops and 47 kilometres — Saint-Jean-Cap-Ferrat Peninsula Loop, Maugham tried to adopt his secretary to secure legacy and Cap Ferrat, meeting a 16-year-old French courtesan in 1900. There is also a tour of Port Grimaud nearby; if you would like to visit a museum, the Musee Picasso is nearby.
